specPoints.text: understand the following reactions: i solid Group 1 halides with concentrated sulfuric acid, to illustrate the trend in reducing ability of the hydrogen halides ii precipitation reactions of the aqueous anions Cl - , Br - and I - with aqueous silver nitrate solution and nitric acid, and the solubility of the precipitates in aqueous ammonia solution iii hydrogen halides with ammonia gas (to produce ammonium halides) and with water (to produce acids)

be able to make predictions about fluorine and astatine and their compounds, in terms of knowledge of trends in halogen chemistry Further suggested practicals: i reaction of solid potassium halides with concentrated sulfuric acid ii precipitation reaction for halides and other anions

primer.text: Concentrated sulfuric acid tests halide grit: chloride only steams, bromide turns the acid to choking dioxide, and iodide pushes sulfur all the way to stinking hydrogen sulfide. This note also equips you with the silver nitrate test and the fluorine and astatine prediction patterns.

lessons.title: Halide ions versus concentrated sulfuric acid: the chloride story
sourceHeadings: Reaction of chloride ions with concentrated sulfuric acid
lessons.opening: Add concentrated sulfuric acid to a solid halide and a toxic gas leaves the test tube. For chloride the story stops at hydrogen chloride - misty fumes in moist air - because chloride is the weakest reducing agent of the trio.
keyPoints: Halide ions meeting concentrated sulfuric acid give off toxic gases, so the reactions belong in a fume cupboard.
The general step is H2SO4 + X- -> HX + HSO4-, producing the hydrogen halide.
With sodium chloride the product is hydrogen chloride gas, seen as misty fumes: H2SO4 + NaCl -> HCl + NaHSO4.
Concentrated sulfuric acid is not reduced by chloride, so the chloride reaction stops at the hydrogen halide.

low.restatement: Every halide first grabs a proton from sulfuric acid to make the hydrogen halide; with chloride nothing further happens - just misty HCl fumes in the moist air.
low.analogy: A weak thief (chloride) picks the pocket (proton) but cannot rob the vault (the acid's own atoms) - the strongest acid reagent stays intact.
low.examPointer: State the observation 'misty fumes of hydrogen chloride' and write the NaCl equation with NaHSO4 as the second product.

medium.restatement: The first step is acid-base: the halide acts as a base, taking H+ from H2SO4 to give HX and HSO4-. Chloride's low reducing power means no subsequent redox with the acid, which is why only steamy fumes appear.
medium.analogy: The first handshake (proton transfer) completes; the stronger handshake (electron transfer) never happens for chloride.
medium.examPointer: Do not invent bromine or sulfur dioxide for the chloride tube - those belong to bromide and iodide.

check.stem: Why are these reactions carried out in a fume cupboard?

options.text: The reactions produce toxic gases
options.explanation: Hydrogen halides and their oxidation products are toxic, so fumes must be contained.

options.text: The acid is highly flammable
options.explanation: Concentrated sulfuric acid is corrosive but not flammable.

options.text: The solids react explosively
options.explanation: The reaction is steady gas evolution, not explosive.

options.text: The products are radioactive
options.explanation: No radioactivity is involved.

check.stem: The general first step of halide ion with concentrated sulfuric acid produces

options.text: The hydrogen halide HX plus the hydrogensulfate ion
options.explanation: H2SO4 + X- -> HX + HSO4- is the shared opening move for all three halides.

options.text: Sulfur dioxide and water directly
options.explanation: SO2 appears only when the acid is reduced, which chloride never achieves.

options.text: The metal sulfate and hydrogen gas
options.explanation: Hydrogen gas is not a product of these reactions.

options.text: A silver halide precipitate
options.explanation: That belongs to silver nitrate tests, not sulfuric acid reactions.

check.stem: The observation when concentrated sulfuric acid meets solid sodium chloride is

options.text: Misty fumes of hydrogen chloride gas
options.explanation: HCl gas steams in moist air as the classic misty fumes.

options.text: Reddish-brown gas of bromine
options.explanation: Bromine belongs to the bromide reaction.

options.text: Yellow solid of sulfur
options.explanation: Sulfur deposition happens with iodide, not chloride.

options.text: A loud pop as hydrogen ignites
options.explanation: No hydrogen forms in this reaction.

check.stem: Chloride does not reduce concentrated sulfuric acid because

options.text: Chloride is the weakest reducing agent of the three common halides
options.explanation: Its electrons are held too firmly for the acid to be pushed into reduction products.

options.text: Sulfuric acid cannot accept electrons at all
options.explanation: The acid is reduced by bromide and iodide, so it clearly can.

options.text: The misty fumes block electron transfer
options.explanation: Fumes are an observation, not a mechanism.

options.text: Chloride is too large to approach the acid
options.explanation: Chloride is smaller than bromide and iodide.

check.stem: The second product beside HCl in the NaCl reaction is

options.text: Sodium hydrogensulfate, NaHSO4
options.explanation: The remaining HSO4- pairs with the sodium to give NaHSO4.

options.text: Sodium sulfate, Na2SO4
options.explanation: That would need two sodium ions; the equation shows NaHSO4.

options.text: Sodium chloride solution
options.explanation: The NaCl is consumed, not regenerated.

options.text: Sodium oxide
options.explanation: No oxide forms under these conditions.

check.stem: Write the equation for sodium chloride with concentrated sulfuric acid.
check.modelAnswer: H2SO4 (l) + NaCl (s) -> HCl (g) + NaHSO4 (s), the misty-fume reaction.

check.stem: State the safety requirement for halide-sulfuric acid reactions.
check.modelAnswer: They must be carried out in a fume cupboard because toxic gases are produced.

check.stem: Explain why only misty fumes are seen with chloride, with no further products.
check.modelAnswer: Chloride's weak reducing power cannot push concentrated sulfuric acid into redox, so the acid-base step to HCl is the entire reaction.

check.stem: A student adds concentrated sulfuric acid to solid NaCl and smells nothing but sees steamy fumes. Name the gas and state why a damp blue litmus test near the mouth of the tube turns red.
check.modelAnswer: The gas is hydrogen chloride; it dissolves in the damp litmus to give hydrochloric acid, whose H+ turns the indicator red - confirming an acidic, water-soluble gas.

lessons.title: Bromide and iodide: the acid gets reduced
sourceHeadings: Reaction of bromide ions with concentrated sulfuric acid
Reaction of iodide ions with concentrated sulfuric acid
lessons.opening: Down the group the halide's reducing power climbs. Bromide strips the acid down to sulfur dioxide and reddish-brown bromine; iodide goes further still, to sulfur, even to rotten-egg hydrogen sulfide, as violet iodine vapour pours out.
keyPoints: Hydrogen halides lose thermal stability descending the group, so HBr and HI decompose further.
Bromide: H2SO4 + NaBr -> HBr + NaHSO4, then 2HBr + H2SO4 -> Br2 + SO2 + 2H2O, giving a reddish-brown gas.
Iodide: HI is oxidised by the acid to I2 with SO2, then further to yellow solid sulfur (6HI) and to hydrogen sulfide (8HI).
Hydrogen sulfide betrays itself with a strong smell of bad eggs.

low.restatement: Bromide stops the acid at SO2 plus bromine vapour; iodide keeps going - SO2, then yellow sulfur, then stinking H2S - because iodide donates electrons ever more readily.
low.analogy: Bromide picks one lock; iodide is a master key opening the acid's vault down to the deepest (-2 sulfur) floor.
low.examPointer: Know all three iodide equations (2, 6, 8 HI) and the observations: purple vapour, yellow solid, bad-egg smell.

medium.restatement: Each hydrogen halide first forms as before; then the acid oxidises it while being reduced itself: sulfur +6 -> +4 (SO2), -> 0 (S), -> -2 (H2S). The iodide route reaches the deepest reduction because iodide is the strongest reducing agent here.
medium.analogy: The acid's sulfur atom descends a three-floor ladder (+6 to +4 to 0 to -2) as the halide climbs its own reactivity ladder.
medium.examPointer: Match each observation to its equation: SO2 choking gas, Br2 reddish-brown, I2 violet, S yellow solid, H2S bad eggs.

check.stem: Which gas confirms that bromide reduces concentrated sulfuric acid?

options.text: Sulfur dioxide, alongside reddish-brown bromine vapour
options.explanation: 2HBr + H2SO4 -> Br2 + SO2 + 2H2O shows the acid reduced to +4 sulfur.

options.text: Hydrogen sulfide with a bad egg smell
options.explanation: H2S needs iodide's stronger reducing power.

options.text: Steamy fumes only, with nothing else
options.explanation: Fumes alone would mean no reduction, which is chloride's case.

options.text: Oxygen gas from decomposed acid
options.explanation: Oxygen is not among the products.

check.stem: The yellow solid seen in the iodide reaction is

options.text: Sulfur, from the acid reduced all the way to oxidation state 0
options.explanation: 6HI + H2SO4 -> 3I2 + S + 4H2O deposits yellow sulfur.

options.text: Iodine, precipitating from solution
options.explanation: Iodine appears as violet vapour, not a yellow solid.

options.text: Sodium iodide crystals
options.explanation: NaI was the starting solid.

options.text: Sodium hydrogensulfate, always yellow
options.explanation: NaHSO4 forms in every halide reaction and is not the diagnostic yellow deposit.

check.stem: Hydrogen sulfide forms in the iodide reaction when

options.text: Eight HI molecules supply enough electrons to drop sulfur to -2
options.explanation: 8HI + H2SO4 -> 4I2 + H2S + 4H2O reaches the acid's deepest reduction.

options.text: Two HI react with the acid
options.explanation: The 2HI step stops at sulfur dioxide.

options.text: The acid oxidises iodide to iodate
options.explanation: No iodate forms; the iodine is at 0 in I2.

options.text: Water reacts with the remaining acid
options.explanation: Water is a product throughout, not a reagent here.

check.stem: Why does HI decompose more readily than HCl?

options.text: The thermal stability of hydrogen halides decreases down the group
options.explanation: Larger, weaker H-X bonds break more easily, so HI decomposes easiest.

options.text: HI is more polar than HCl
options.explanation: Polarity actually decreases down the group.

options.text: Iodine is a stronger oxidising agent than chlorine
options.explanation: Iodine is weaker; the stability trend runs on bond strength.

options.text: Hydrogen iodide is ionic while HCl is covalent
options.explanation: Both are covalent molecular gases.

check.stem: The SO2 formed from iodide can be reduced further, demonstrating

options.text: Iodide's maximum reducing power, unseen with chloride or bromide
options.explanation: SO2 + 6HI -> H2S + 3I2 + 2H2O shows iodide pushing sulfur to -2.

options.text: That sulfur dioxide is a reducing agent toward iodide
options.explanation: SO2 is the species being reduced here, not the reducer.

options.text: That the acid regenerates itself after reduction
options.explanation: The acid is consumed into reduction products.

options.text: A gas solubility effect rather than redox
options.explanation: The sulfur oxidation state changes, so it is redox.

check.stem: Write the equation for the bromide-SO2 step.
State the observation that identifies hydrogen sulfide.
check.modelAnswer: A strong smell of bad eggs identifies H2S gas.

check.stem: Explain why iodide produces more reduction products than bromide.
check.modelAnswer: Iodide is a stronger reducing agent than bromide because its outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more easily donated, so it can reduce sulfuric acid beyond SO2 to sulfur and even hydrogen sulfide.

check.stem: Three unlabelled solids are NaCl, NaBr and NaI. Concentrated sulfuric acid gives misty fumes with A, reddish-brown gas plus choking gas with B, and purple vapour plus yellow solid with C. Identify all three.
check.modelAnswer: A is NaCl (HCl misty fumes only), B is NaBr (HBr then Br2 and SO2), C is NaI (HI decomposed by the acid to violet I2 vapour, yellow sulfur and beyond).

lessons.title: The reducing-power ladder and the silver nitrate test
sourceHeadings: Explaining the Trend in Reducing Ability of Halide Ions
lessons.opening: Two ladders meet here: halide reducing power climbing Cl- < Br- < I-, and the silver nitrate test reading back from precipitate colour and ammonia solubility to the halide identity.
keyPoints: Halide reducing power increases down the group as the ions get larger and their outer electrons are lost more readily.
Silver nitrate gives ionic AgX precipitates: Ag+ + X- -> AgX, in colours white (chloride), cream (bromide), pale yellow (iodide).
Ammonia distinguishes the precipitates: chloride dissolves in dilute ammonia, bromide only in concentrated, iodide in neither.

low.restatement: Bigger halide ions lose electrons more easily, so reducing power runs Cl- < Br- < I-. In testing, silver halide colours deepen from white through cream to pale yellow, and ammonia strength needed to dissolve them runs the same way down.
low.analogy: Three locks of increasing stubbornness: the chloride lock opens with a light key (dilute ammonia), bromide needs the heavy key, iodide refuses both.
low.examPointer: Quote the full test sequence - nitric acid, silver nitrate, then dilute then concentrated ammonia - and match every colour and solubility outcome.

medium.restatement: Electron loss ease grows with ionic radius because the outer electrons feel less nuclear pull; that is why iodide can reduce SO2 while chloride cannot. The silver test works independently of redox: Ag+ precipitates AgX, and ammonia complexes the silver, dissolving the precipitate according to halide.
medium.analogy: The ammonia key unlocks silver from its halide partner; the deeper the lock (heavier halide), the stronger the key needed.
medium.examPointer: Nitric acid first removes interfering ions such as carbonate - do not omit it in the written method.

check.stem: The order of halide reducing power is

options.text: Cl- < Br- < I-
options.explanation: Increasing size down the group makes electron loss easier, so iodide is the strongest reducing agent.

options.text: I- < Br- < Cl-
options.explanation: That reverses the radius-based trend.

options.text: All equal, as each carries one negative charge
options.explanation: Identical charge does not mean identical electron-donating ease.

options.text: Cl- < I- < Br-
options.explanation: Iodide sits at the top of the ladder, not in the middle.

check.stem: Larger halide ions are stronger reducing agents because

options.text: Their outer electrons are further from the nucleus and so more easily lost
options.explanation: Weaker nuclear pull on the expanded outer shell lowers the cost of electron donation.

options.text: They have more protons attracting electrons
options.explanation: More protons would make electron loss harder, not easier.

options.text: They are lighter and move faster
options.explanation: Mass and speed are not the mechanism here.

options.text: They carry a double negative charge
options.explanation: All three carry a single negative charge.

check.stem: Adding silver nitrate to a solution containing iodide gives

options.text: A pale yellow precipitate of silver iodide
options.explanation: AgI is the pale yellow precipitate of the trio.

options.text: A white precipitate
options.explanation: White is silver chloride.

options.text: A cream precipitate
options.explanation: Cream is silver bromide.

options.text: No precipitate, as AgI is soluble
options.explanation: AgI is insoluble; only AgF is soluble.

check.stem: A precipitate dissolves in concentrated ammonia but not in dilute ammonia. The halide is

options.text: Bromide, whose cream AgBr needs concentrated ammonia
options.explanation: The dilute-insoluble, concentrated-soluble pattern is unique to bromide.

options.text: Chloride, which dissolves even in dilute ammonia
options.explanation: Chloride dissolves at the first ammonia step.

options.text: Iodide, which dissolves in neither
options.explanation: AgI stays insoluble in both.

options.text: Fluoride, since AgF precipitates first
options.explanation: AgF is soluble, so no precipitate forms at all.

check.stem: Nitric acid is added before the silver nitrate because it

options.text: Removes interfering ions such as carbonate that would also give precipitates
options.explanation: Acidifying first clears the field so only halides precipitate with Ag+.

options.text: Oxidises the halide ions to halogens
options.explanation: The acid's job is to clear interferents, not oxidise halides.

options.text: Dissolves the silver nitrate
options.explanation: Silver nitrate dissolves in water unaided.

options.text: Neutralises the ammonia added later
options.explanation: The ammonia comes after; the acid step precedes the silver.

check.stem: State the colours of the three silver halide precipitates.
check.modelAnswer: Silver chloride is white, silver bromide is cream, and silver iodide is pale yellow.

check.stem: State the ammonia solubility pattern of the silver halides.
check.modelAnswer: AgCl dissolves in dilute ammonia; AgBr dissolves only in concentrated ammonia; AgI dissolves in neither.

check.stem: Explain why reducing power and the depth of sulfuric acid reduction rise together down the group.
check.modelAnswer: Both trends measure electron donation: the easier a halide loses electrons (larger ion, weaker pull), the further it can push the acid's sulfur down its oxidation ladder.

check.stem: A solution forms a cream precipitate with silver nitrate that will not dissolve in dilute ammonia but does in concentrated ammonia. Which halide is present, and which observation would the halide-sulfuric acid test show?
check.modelAnswer: Bromide is present; with concentrated sulfuric acid it would give misty HBr fumes followed by a reddish-brown gas of bromine and choking sulfur dioxide.

lessons.title: Hydrogen halides, fluorine and astatine predictions
lessons.opening: Hydrogen halides are the group's acids in waiting: they meet ammonia to give ammonium salts and water to give the hydrohalic acids. Fluorine and astatine extend the ladder - with exceptions like soluble silver fluoride that keep predictions honest.
keyPoints: Halogen with hydrogen gives the hydrogen halide, e.g. Cl2 + H2 -> 2HCl.
Hydrogen halides react with ammonia to form ammonium halides, e.g. NH3 + HCl -> NH4Cl.
In water, hydrogen chloride ionises into hydrochloric acid: HCl -> H+ + Cl-.
Silver fluoride is soluble, so silver nitrate cannot test for fluoride; predictions for astatine follow the group pattern.

low.restatement: Hydrogen halides split two ways: with ammonia they crystallise as ammonium salts; in water they ionise into the acids. Fluorine and astatine slots into the group pattern, with the noted silver fluoride exception.
low.analogy: One molecule, two doors: the ammonia door yields a solid salt, the water door yields free ions that conduct and turn litmus red.
low.examPointer: For astatide questions, mirror iodide chemistry and adjust one step down the group; remember AgF's solubility when asked about fluoride tests.

medium.restatement: Acid formation in water is ionisation: HX releases H+ (as H3O+) and X-. For hydrogen astatide the same pattern applies, HAt + H2O -> H3O+ + At-. The fluoride exception arises because AgF does not precipitate, so the standard halide test fails for fluoride.
medium.analogy: Every hydrogen halide drops its proton into water the same way; astatine is just the next rung of the same ladder.
medium.examPointer: Write astatide equations by pattern-matching iodide, and quote AgF(aq) as the soluble exception when fluoride testing is asked.

check.stem: Hydrogen chloride reacting with ammonia gas forms

options.text: Solid ammonium chloride, NH4Cl
options.explanation: NH3 + HCl -> NH4Cl, the classic white smoke of ammonium halide formation.

options.text: Nitrogen and hydrogen gases
options.explanation: No decomposition to elements occurs.

options.text: Chloramine and water
options.explanation: That is not the ammonium halide chemistry here.

options.text: Aqueous ammonium ions only
options.explanation: In dry gas the product is the solid salt.

check.stem: Dissolving hydrogen chloride in water gives

options.text: Hydrochloric acid, with H+ and Cl- in solution
options.explanation: HCl -> H+ + Cl- is the ionisation that makes the acid.

options.text: Chlorine gas and hydrogen gas
options.explanation: No gases form; the molecules ionise.

options.text: Chlorate(I) acid
options.explanation: That is the chlorine-water disproportionation product, different chemistry.

options.text: A neutral solution of molecular HCl
options.explanation: The acid ionises, so the solution is strongly acidic.

check.stem: Why can silver nitrate not test for fluoride ions?

options.text: Silver fluoride is soluble, so no precipitate forms
options.explanation: Ag+ + F- -> AgF(aq) stays in solution, giving no visible change.

options.text: Fluoride is too reactive to remain in solution
options.explanation: Fluoride ions are stable in water; the issue is silver salt solubility.

options.text: Silver fluoride is white and indistinguishable from chloride
options.explanation: The real problem is that it never precipitates at all.

options.text: Fluoride decomposes the silver nitrate
options.explanation: No such decomposition happens.

check.stem: Predicting astatine chemistry from the group pattern, hydrogen astatide in water forms

options.text: Hydronium ions and astatide ions, by analogy with HI
options.explanation: HAt + H2O -> H3O+ + At- follows the hydrogen iodide pattern one step down.

options.text: Astatine molecules and hydrogen gas
options.explanation: No redox to elements occurs in the ionisation.

options.text: An insoluble astatide precipitate
options.explanation: Ionisation, not precipitation, describes the acid formation.

options.text: No reaction, as astatine is inert
options.explanation: Astatine follows the group pattern for prediction purposes.

check.stem: Halogen meeting hydrogen demonstrates that

options.text: Halogen plus hydrogen gives the hydrogen halide in 1:1 molecule ratio
options.explanation: One chlorine molecule reacts with one hydrogen molecule to make two HCl.

options.text: Hydrogen reduces the halogen to hydride
options.explanation: The halogen is reduced to -1 inside HCl, but the reaction is formation, not hydride chemistry.

options.text: Chlorine acts as a reducing agent here
options.explanation: Chlorine gains electrons; it is the oxidising agent.

options.text: The reaction needs a catalyst of ammonia
options.explanation: Ammonia reacts with the product later; no catalyst is involved.

check.stem: Write the equation for ammonia with hydrogen chloride gas.
check.modelAnswer: NH3 (g) + HCl (g) -> NH4Cl (s), forming the ammonium chloride salt.

check.stem: State the exception that blocks the fluoride halide test.
check.modelAnswer: Silver fluoride is soluble, so acidified silver nitrate gives no precipitate for fluoride.

check.stem: Explain how the group pattern supports predicting astatide reactions.
check.modelAnswer: Astatine sits below iodine, so its ions and acids mirror iodide behaviour one rung down the group - same equations with At replacing I, adjusted for its position.

check.stem: Hydrogen astatide gas dissolves in water. Write the equation and predict the effect on damp litmus paper.
check.modelAnswer: HAt (g) + H2O (l) -> H3O+ (aq) + At- (aq); the released H3O+ turns damp blue litmus red, as with any hydrohalic acid.

glossary.definition: A binary compound of hydrogen with a halogen, HX, which fumes in moist air and ionises to a hydrohalic acid in water.
A species that donates electrons to another species, reducing it while being oxidised itself.
The HSO4- ion left when sulfuric acid donates one proton to a halide ion.
The resistance of a hydrogen halide to decomposition; it decreases down the group, so HI breaks apart most readily.

workedExample.prompt: Hydrogen astatide gas is bubbled into water and an acid forms. Write the equation for the ionisation.
steps: Model the ionisation on hydrogen iodide: HI (g) + H2O (l) -> H3O+ (aq) + I- (aq).
Substitute astatine one place below iodine in the group pattern.
Check the charge ledger: neutral reactants give one positive and one negative ion, and H, O and At atom counts balance.
